PAs are nerve-wrecking since each one is worth almost as much as the midterm. So triple-whammy.

Midterm focused on algorithm dry runs / numpy functions / pros & cons of algorithms & parameter choices / the reasoning behind certain steps in algorithms. Familiarizing yourself with the slides should be fine.

Final is much more nightmarish. Each question has like 10 subquestions, eaching worth 0.5 - 2 points.
You will be doing questions after questions, thinking when is this topic's question over.
Dry-running a full perceptron epoch (time-consuming & one mistake & mistakes cascades) is only worth 3-4 points.
The CNN question was a killer, worth 25 in total. 16 are dedicated to subquestions about a CNN variant that you have not been taught before. You need to understand how it works (dry-run), find specific kernels (like identify matrices in MATH2111), and write logical proof (COMP2711 & COMP3711).
Since I have taken COMP2711, COMP3711 and MATH2111, my math & algorithm logic foundation is decent and I managed fine. But I can see someone who is not used to this feeling petrified.
sections.workload:
- Attendance
Out of 11 labs, 10 labs requires attendance.
TAs will scan ID cards at the start of the labs, so you have to show up, though some people just leave right after. No iPRS.

- Assignments
5 out of 11 labs are graded, but only the best 4 will be counted. Theoretically, you can skip the last graded lab if you have got 100% in the first 4. But something happened that caused the grading of the Lab 8 to be delayed after the deadline of Lab 10, so had to do all 5 to play safe for this semester.

Compared to the labs / PA in COMP2011/2012, it is definitely more annoying.

In the early labs, there are often constraints (e.g. no explicit loops; no nested loops, efficiency). They are useful to get used to the numpy library, but it may take some time to figure out how to do so. Though exams do often ask for one-line code using numpy, so better get used to it.

The later labs and PAs are the most different from the typical COMP assignments. Instead of judging based on sample output, you are graded on whether your AI model accuracy is above a threshold. So you have to time to fine tune the parameters.
The AI models takes time to train (at least 2-5 minutes), so don't expect to hit compile and get output like COMP2011/2012.

Difficulty is fine, just expect to need to spend more time to get the assignments done.

Overall all topics are covered at a depth to rouse interest in AI but not so deep such that it becomes too advanced. One main critique of previous versions of the course was only teaching scikit-learn and keras as the ML frameworks for this course, which are hardly used in actual projects. However, due to the introduction of COMP1023, numpy is no longer taught in this course (although it is still assessed) and deep learning with pytorch is instead taught. Pytorch is a very useful framework for ML-related projects (e.g. in UROP) so I would say the content is A+ now.

Initially I was in Xiao Huiru's class. She teaches ok but I didn't see the point in attending her lectures since you can just get the same information faster by reading the slides. However, due to some conflicts with schedule, I later swapped to Desmond's class, but I still didn't attend due to my experience with Ms. Xiao's class.

As you can tell from reading other reviews, this was a huge mistake on my part. Because pytorch was a new topic (and hence not in past papers), I decided to watch the recordings for pytorch and omg Desmond teaches so well. He adds so much more in his lectures than just the content of the slides. The slides themselves are very good but Desmond explains every tiny little detail on how and why everything is the way it is. His explanation on one-hot encode blew my mind. Even though I got A+, I 100% regret not attending Desmond's lectures because my understanding of the content would be at least 10x clearer. Now if you only care about getting a good grade, you could skip lectures to save time, but if you really want to learn, you should never skip Desmond's lecture (this is coming from someone who almost never attends any lecture from any course btw; he is just that good). I see why he is ranked #1 on UST Rankings.

Good course as an intro to almost every 4000-level AI course, but not very good grade as we heard because this course have too many strong and competitive people eating all of the A range.

Starting from this semester, this course is renamed from "Exploring Artificial Intelligence" to "Introduction to Artificial Intelligence". The content covered in this semester also have a remarkable reform: covered PyTorch (though I think it seems like learning nothing, just like matplotlib in COMP1023, you can simply learn this on the exam), and removed the introduction to advanced python (since it is moved to COMP1023).

The content outline:
- Naive Bayes Classifier
- K-Nearest Neighbours, K-Means Clustering
- Image Processing
- ANN, MLP, CNN using Keras and Tensorflow
- PyTorch (new!!)
- Minimax and Alpha-Beta Pruning
- AI Ethics

so you can see, this course provide a strong foundation for you to step in advanced AI course like COMP4211, COMP4221, COMP4471. Sadly, Desmond still didn't release (need to fact check) the recording introducing about Reinforcement Learning. If do so, this course can also provide a prerequisite to the new course (not new?) COMP4212 - Reinforcement Learning.

However, in my opinion, it is still encouraged to take COMP2711/H before taking this course? As this course is still, an semi-math course but not something practical (although this course is aimed to provide a background of AI code for those advanced AI course, but still, we need to learn the mathematical background of those AI algorithms). Taking COMP2711/H is helpful for you to provide a mathematical background to take this course (epspecially the Bayes Theorem for Naive Bayes Classifier).

Update on 15/9/2026 (9up moment again):

For those who are curious about what is gradient descent, Desmond is really nice to share his supplementary note about deriving that. However, you need to self-study them as Desmond will not teach this during lecture, and you better should know what is multivariable calculus (maybe take 2023/2024 as a corequisite of it so that would be better?)

In addition, having a linear algebra background (or say matrix multiplication) would be helpful for you to deal with some problems related to numpy and understand the code in MLP.
sections.teaching:
Desmond should be an A++ lecturer. He teach everything in a very attractive teaching style, always very energetic and patient. In my opinion, he is already the best lecturer in CSE (same as my opinion to Sunil). He always provide a classical, illustrative example to students. In his lecture, you won't be bored because of the content, and also: even you are not focus to what Desmond said during lecture, you will also have some feel when you start revision. He also allows student to raise their hands and share their own opinion during lectures, or find him to discuss after lecture or in his office during his office hour.

However, talking about course materials: PPT are not self-contained enough and with an anti-self-study design. You are required to attend the lectures / watch the lecture recordings (still recommend Desmond one because the PPT is most likely designed by him), because skipping lectures makes you difficult to understand the logic behind the bullet points. If you think you can just be a free-rider, skip lectures, and cram by reading the PPTs before the final, I encourage you, my dearest children, please don't.

Later on, we can use libraries like SciKitLearn and Keras, BUT fine-tuning the training model hyperparameters will take the majority of the time instead of coding.

= The code =
The programs were saved in Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb) and executed on Google Colab. No setup is required for GColab but for later labs where you need to train a model, you need to be wary of the limited GPU usage quota. If you have a decent PC, I highly recommend setting up your local Anaconda environment and VSCode so that you can train on your own GPU w/ Tensorflow GPU (which in my Lab 8 is 4s/epoch on RTX3060 compared to 11s/epoch on GColab's Nvidea T4). Yes, it will be quite a hassle, but you will thank it for speeding up training by a margin and allowing you to test more model configurations.
▷ Anaconda Navigator: https://docs.anaconda.com/free/navigator/index.html
(Note that Tensorflow GPU needs to specifically be installed through your environment's terminal and then "pip -install tensorflow-gpu". It might be different for you, but that's how I got mine working)

An introductory course to A.I. I tend to divide the course into four parts:

Personal comment:

1. Before Naive Bayes, an introduction to Python is given (with many extra lessons!) Therefore there is no need to worry if you are not familiar with Python.
2. This is really an introductory course, in the sense that the requirement of math is even fewer than Andrew Ng's AI course in Coursera... But I find this course better anyway.
3. The part for reinforcement learning is actually a good starter to learn (discrete time) "stochastic process", which is an interesting topic in math. I personally find the related material in this course is more readable than that in MATH3425...
sections.teaching:
1. Enthusiasm: Desmond's enthusiasm in teaching makes the class lively. Because of that, this is the first course that I seldom feel bored or refused to attend the F2F class.

sections.grading:
1. As usual, Desmond's course promises as large A range as possible.
2. Warning: This semester is more competitive than the last one! Given that the midterm exams in two semesters are about the same (in terms of style, difficulty...), last sem's mean is ~65, and this sem's mean is ~80...
3. However, the final exam in this semester is much harder. It requires deeper understanding (than last sem's final paper) to get high score, and there are more parts requiring you to hand-write codes.

sections.workload:
Assignments: Only 5 labs and 2 programming assignments are required to submit. The labs are simple.

The only tricky assignment in this semester is PA1: It requires you to do modification to your code well to get full score, which strictly needs to apply vectorization everywhere instead of loops; PA2 is another extreme: You even do not have to think because the architecture is given - Because of that, this PA is even easier than regular lab...

Preparation for exam: Since necessary math formulas and codes commands are given in exam, the only thing which is essential to memorize is the rationale behind each algorithm. Indeed there are some other tricky things like broadcasting rule, do convolution or calculating number of trainable parameters and so on, but they can be understood once you are willing to practice.
